title: Failed RDMA teardown does not authorize freeing DMA buffers
applies_when: A native-resource leak hypothesis proposes continuing cleanup after QP destruction or memory-region deregistration fails. Trace the owning destructor, retirement/retry path and buffer dependencies, not only the early return.
lesson: A failed release may leave a device reference alive. Before freeing its backing memory, establish successful deregistration or another documented quiescence guarantee. At the cited Mooncake revision, closeNotification preserves failed QP/MR handles and returns before buffer reset; the owning destructor explicitly retains the DMA buffers on teardown failure. finishDestroy retries deconstructLocked, and its outstanding-work gate preserves retired endpoints. Destroying independent ordinary QPs in a loop does not justify freeing their dependent state or notification buffers after failure. Compare a successful release, a failed dependency release and a later successful retry when designing a native reproduction.
avoid_when: This is source evidence of intentional retention, not proof that all Mooncake teardown is correct or leak-free, a native RDMA failure-injection result, or a universal recommendation to leak on error. Reclaiming an independent resource may be safe after proving its exact lifetime; the send-MR failure alone does not prove that recv-MR deregistration must be skipped. Reopen with an actual supported path, resource dependency and safe reclaim guarantee. A mock observing another cleanup call does not establish hardware quiescence.

evidence.note: The destructor deliberately releases owning smart pointers without deleting the DMA buffers after deconstructLocked fails; it documents the safety boundary. Source inspection only.
Retirement waits for outstanding work and retries failed teardown. This contradicts the truncated-source claim that no owner retry exists, without proving every provider failure is recoverable.
Notification teardown clears successful handles but returns on failed QP destruction or MR deregistration before resetting backing buffers.
